claim: Primary visual cortex (V1) in the mouse projects to numerous brain areas, including several secondary visual areas, frontal cortex, and basal ganglia.
source: Primary visual cortex (V1) in the mouse projects to numerous brain areas, including several secondary visual areas, frontal cortex, and basal ganglia.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work establishing anatomical connectivity patterns.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of V1 strongly impairs visually guided behavior.
source: While it has been demonstrated that optogenetic silencing of V1 strongly impairs visually guided behavior, it is not known which downstream areas are required for visual behaviors.
evidence: This is stated as an established finding from prior research, setting up the motivation for the current study.

claim: Activity in secondary visual areas is required for a simple visual contrast-increment change detection task.
source: Optogenetic silencing of visual responses in secondary visual areas revealed that their activity is required for even this simple visual task.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by behavioral experiments with optogenetic manipulation.

claim: Inhibiting secondary visual areas produces profound suppression at the location of the optogenetic light.
source: In vivo electrophysiology showed that, although inhibiting secondary visual areas could produce some feedback effects in V1, the principal effect was profound suppression at the location of the optogenetic light.
evidence: This finding is based on electrophysiological recordings during optogenetic manipulation.

claim: Pathways through secondary visual areas are necessary for even simple visual behaviors.
source: The results show that pathways through secondary visual areas are necessary for even simple visual behaviors.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the behavioral and physiological data presented in the study.

claim: The borders and locations of mouse visual areas were initially identified through reversals in retinotopy.
source: The borders and locations of mouse visual areas were initially identified through reversals in retinotopy (Dräger, 1975; Wagor et al., 1980) and cytoarchitecture (Caviness, 1975).
evidence: This statement references historical work on mapping mouse visual areas.

claim: V1 projects to several secondary (higher) visual areas.
source: Later, injections of anterograde tracers into V1 showed that V1 projects to several secondary (higher) visual areas (Wang and Burkhalter, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to anatomical tracing studies.

claim: As many as 16 individual, retinotopically mapped areas have been identified in mouse visual cortex.
source: These imaging studies have identified as many as 16 individual, retinotopically mapped areas (Zhuang et al., 2017) that vary in the strength of their connectivity to V1.
evidence: This is based on a citation to a comprehensive mapping study.

claim: More than half of V1 projections target four secondary visual areas: LM, AL, RL, and PM.
source: While more than half of V1 projections target these four secondary visual areas (Han et al., 2018), V1 also projects to a number of other brain areas including frontal cortex and basal ganglia (Han et al., 2018; Khibnik et al., 2014), both of which are involved in decision-making and action selection.
evidence: This quantitative anatomical claim is supported by citations to connectivity studies.

claim: V1 also projects to frontal cortex and basal ganglia, which are involved in decision-making and action selection.
source: While more than half of V1 projections target these four secondary visual areas (Han et al., 2018), V1 also projects to a number of other brain areas including frontal cortex and basal ganglia (Han et al., 2018; Khibnik et al., 2014), both of which are involved in decision-making and action selection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Neural activity in V1 carries substantial information about visual stimulus contrast.
source: Neural activity in V1 carries substantial information about visual stimulus contrast (Albrecht and Hamilton, 1982; Sclar et al., 1990; Vaiceliunaite et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to physiological studies of V1 contrast responses.

claim: Neurons in mouse V1 are tuned for oriented visual stimuli, with a tuning curve that peaks at the cell's preferred orientation.
source: Neurons in mouse V1 are tuned for oriented visual stimuli, with a tuning curve that peaks at the cell's preferred orientation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about V1 physiology.

claim: As stimulus contrast increases, single V1 neurons increase their firing rates monotonically.
source: The same neurons simultaneously encode contrast: as stimulus contrast increases, single V1 neurons increase their firing rates monotonically (Busse et al., 2011; Glickfeld et al., 2013a; Khastkhodaei et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of contrast response functions in mouse V1.

claim: The average V1 response does not completely saturate, even up to 100% contrast.
source: As expected from single neurons' responses, the average, or summed, V1 response does not completely saturate, even up to 100% contrast (Glickfeld et al., 2013a; Histed, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of population responses in V1.

claim: Linear decoders that do not take trial-to-trial variability into account perform well on decoding orientation from mouse V1.
source: While the structure of population neural variability could, in principle, make linear decoding difficult, linear decoders that do not take trial-to-trial variability into account perform well on decoding orientation from mouse V1 (Berens et al., 2012; Rumyantsev et al., 2020; Stringer et al., 2019; Kafashan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to computational studies of V1 population coding.

claim: Suppressing V1 optogenetically produces retinotopically-specific impairments in contrast-detection performance.
source: This task was previously found to require V1; suppressing V1 optogenetically produced retinotopically-specific impairments in contrast-detection performance (Glickfeld et al., 2013b; Jin and Glickfeld, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior optogenetic studies.

claim: Inhibiting V1 negatively affects perceptual performance in the contrast-change detection task.
source: We found that inhibiting V1 in this way negatively affects perceptual performance.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study's behavioral experiments.

claim: Suppressing lateral areas (e.g., LM/AL and RL) negatively affects performance in the contrast-change detection task.
source: We then inhibited secondary visual areas and found that suppressing lateral areas (e.g., LM/AL and RL) and medial areas (PM) also negatively affects performance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Suppressing medial area PM negatively affects performance in the contrast-change detection task.
source: We then inhibited secondary visual areas and found that suppressing lateral areas (e.g., LM/AL and RL) and medial areas (PM) also negatively affects performance.
evidence: This is stated as a finding, though later the manuscript clarifies that PM effects are weaker than lateral area effects.

claim: Inhibiting secondary visual areas primarily acts to suppress secondary area visual responses, rather than suppressing V1 responses via feedback.
source: Via electrophysiology and widefield calcium imaging, we found that inhibiting secondary visual areas primarily acts to suppress secondary area visual responses, rather than suppressing V1 responses via feedback.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological and imaging data comparing direct and feedback effects.

claim: The effect size caused by suppressing secondary areas can be large, comparable to what is seen when suppressing V1 using the same optogenetic light intensity.
source: These data show that secondary visual areas are involved in a task that, in principle, could have been performed by direct V1 readout alone. We also found that the effect size caused by suppressing secondary areas can be large, comparable to what we see when suppressing V1 using the same optogenetic light intensity.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of behavioral effects across areas.

claim: Suppressing PM only weakly affected performance in the contrast-change detection task.
source: In contrast, suppressing PM, the largest medial area, only weakly affected performance.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments comparing effects across areas.

claim: Feedback effects on V1 neural activity were negligible when PM was suppressed.
source: Paralleling these behavioral findings, we found that any feedback effects on V1 neural activity were negligible when PM was suppressed, whereas inhibiting LM produced some feedback suppression of V1 at high light intensity, arguing that activity in LM has some feedback effect on V1 even though the feedback effects cannot alone explain the changes in perception.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings during optogenetic manipulation.

claim: Inhibiting LM produced some feedback suppression of V1 at high light intensity.
source: Paralleling these behavioral findings, we found that any feedback effects on V1 neural activity were negligible when PM was suppressed, whereas inhibiting LM produced some feedback suppression of V1 at high light intensity, arguing that activity in LM has some feedback effect on V1 even though the feedback effects cannot alone explain the changes in perception.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data showing V1 responses during LM inhibition.

claim: Feedback effects from LM to V1 cannot alone explain the changes in perception caused by LM inhibition.
source: Paralleling these behavioral findings, we found that any feedback effects on V1 neural activity were negligible when PM was suppressed, whereas inhibiting LM produced some feedback suppression of V1 at high light intensity, arguing that activity in LM has some feedback effect on V1 even though the feedback effects cannot alone explain the changes in perception.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the magnitude of feedback effects to behavioral effects.

claim: In all areas, the behavioral effects are primarily due to changes in sensitivity (d′) and not false alarm (FA) rates.
source: Finally, in all areas the behavioral effects are primarily due to changes in sensitivity (d′) and not false alarm (FA) rates.
evidence: This is based on signal detection theory analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Lateral secondary visual areas (LM/AL and RL) form an interconnected network with V1 that contributes to performance in simple, visually guided behaviors.
source: In sum, lateral secondary visual areas (LM/AL and RL) form an interconnected network with V1 that contributes to performance in even simple, visually guided behaviors, for which substantial information is available within, and linearly decodable from, V1.
evidence: This is the main conclusion synthesizing behavioral and physiological findings.

claim: VGAT-ChR2-EYFP transgenic mouse line was used to optogenetically stimulate all inhibitory neural classes.
source: We first confirmed that V1 contributes in our task using the VGAT-ChR2-EFYP transgenic mouse line (Zhao et al., 2011) to optogenetically stimulate all inhibitory neural classes.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: Hemodynamic intrinsic-signal imaging was used to identify retinotopic locations within V1.
source: We found the locations of areas in visual cortex using hemodynamic intrinsic-signal imaging. We identified a series of retinotopic locations within V1 (Materials and methods, Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and based on the location of V1, we identified several secondary visual areas, areas AL, LM, RL, and PM (among the secondary visual areas whose locations are most reliable, Garrett et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental method for area localization.

claim: LED intensities that produced behavioral effects (in V1, 0.43 mW/mm2 to produce a 100% threshold change) completely suppressed neural activity directly under the LED.
source: LED intensities that produced behavioral effects (in V1, 0.43 mW/mm2 to produce a 100% threshold change) completely suppressed neural activity directly under the LED (V1, bootstrap 95% CI 96–100% suppression of visual response without light, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electrophysiological recordings, with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: The half-max radius of suppression (0.73 mm, 95% CI 0.61–0.92) was slightly larger than the half-max radius of the light spots used in the recordings (0.53 ± 0.21 mm, mean ± SD).
source: The half-max radius of suppression (0.73 mm, 95% CI 0.61–0.92) was slightly larger than the half-max radius of the light spots used in the recordings (0.53 ± 0.21 mm, mean ± SD).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electrophysiological measurements of spatial spread.

claim: Peak visual responses were similar in size between V1 and lateral areas, and both were significantly larger than peak responses in PM.
source: Peak visual responses were similar in size between V1 and lateral areas, and both were significantly larger than peak responses in PM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of visual responses across areas, with reference to a figure.

claim: Visual stimulus latency in V1 was measured to be 65 ms (bootstrap 95% CI 63–67 ms).
source: We measured visual stimulus latency (time to half-max response, logistic fit between rmin to rvis) in V1 to be 65 ms (bootstrap 95% CI 63–67 ms).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiological data.

claim: There was a small delay in visual response in the lateral areas relative to V1 (time to half max response = 73 ms, bootstrap 95% CI 70–77 ms).
source: There was a small delay in response in the lateral areas relative to V1 (time to half max response = 73 ms, bootstrap 95% CI 70–77 ms), but a notably larger delay for PM (time to half-max response = 90 ms, bootstrap 95% CI 87–93 ms, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of response latencies across areas.

claim: PM showed a notably larger delay in visual response (time to half-max response = 90 ms, bootstrap 95% CI 87–93 ms) compared to V1 and lateral areas.
source: There was a small delay in response in the lateral areas relative to V1 (time to half max response = 73 ms, bootstrap 95% CI 70–77 ms), but a notably larger delay for PM (time to half-max response = 90 ms, bootstrap 95% CI 87–93 ms, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Inhibiting V1 while recording downstream visual responses in either lateral areas or PM strongly decreased visual responses in both secondary areas.
source: Indeed, inhibiting V1 while recording downstream visual responses in either lateral areas or PM (Figure 6D) strongly decreased visual responses in both secondary areas (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings during optogenetic manipulation.

claim: At light intensities that produced behavioral effects (0.37 mW/mm2), inhibiting LM/AL produced moderate (39%, 95% CI: 24–57%) suppression in V1.
source: At light intensities that produced behavioral effects (0.37 mW/mm2), inhibiting LM/AL produced moderate (39%, 95% CI: 24–57%) suppression in V1.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The same light stimulation (0.37 mW/mm2) nearly eliminated visual responses in LM/AL (i.e., 100% suppression).
source: However, the same light stimulation nearly eliminated visual responses in LM/AL (i.e., 100% suppression).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Suppressing medial areas had little to no feedback effect on V1 visual responses, even at the highest intensities.
source: In contrast to the feedback effects on LM/AL, we found that suppressing medial areas had little to no feedback effect on V1 visual responses, even at the highest intensities (Figure 6H, right).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings during PM inhibition.

claim: When the visual stimulus was paired with LM inhibition, the average V1 response is unchanged.
source: When the visual stimulus was paired with LM inhibition, the average V1 response is unchanged (Figure 6M). (Slight reduction not statistically significant: without LM stimulation V1 response is 1.9% ΔF/F ± 0.22% [mean ± SEM], and with LM stimulation 1.6% ΔF/F ± 0.16%, p for difference = 0.12, Wilcoxon U = 157.0, N1 = 30 trials, N2 = 30, one animal. V1 response is significantly greater than zero, p < 1e-5, Wilcoxon U = 3.0, N = 30 stimuli. Signal is measured in ROI centered on V1 representation; fluorescence is measured in two frames or 200 ms after stimulus onset, relative to fluorescence in two frames before each stimulus onset).
evidence: This is a finding from widefield calcium imaging experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: LM/AL stimulation, and not V1 stimulation, produced large degradation of animals' contrast-change detection behavior when comparing intensities that produced similar V1 suppression.
source: We were then able to examine in our behavioral data how the two types of stimulation (0.08 mW/mm2 to V1; 0.6 mW/mm2 to LM/AL), which affected V1 responses similarly, affected animals' behavior. LM/AL stimulation, and not V1 stimulation, produced large degradation of animals' contrast-change detection behavior (Figure 6N, right).
evidence: This is a comparison of behavioral effects at matched physiological suppression levels.

claim: Feedback suppression of V1 neural activity caused by LM direct inhibition was always two to five times lower than direct suppression of V1 neural activity.
source: We also compared direct and feedback V1 suppression across 0.4–0.8 mm spans of cortex, at both 0.1 and 0.3 mW/mm2, and found that feedback suppression of V1 neural activity caused by LM direct inhibition was always two to five times lower than direct suppression of V1 neural activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: When lateral secondary areas LM/AL are suppressed, it is not the change in V1 responses that drives the behavioral effect.
source: Together, these observations argue that when lateral secondary areas LM/AL are suppressed, it is not the change in V1 responses that drives the behavioral effect, since stimulating V1 itself at an intensity necessary to produce the same V1 change has no effect on perception.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing behavioral effects at matched V1 suppression levels.

claim: It is likely the profound suppression of LM/AL activity (bootstrap 95% CI 99–100% suppression) at 0.6 mW/mm2 that leads to the behavioral degradation.
source: Instead, it is likely the profound suppression of LM/AL activity (bootstrap 95% CI 99–100% suppression) at this light intensity that leads to the behavioral degradation.
evidence: This is an inference from the physiological and behavioral data.

claim: Training animals to perform the task with their ipsilateral forepaw produced similar results as when animals used their contralateral forepaw.
source: Instead, we found that training animals to perform the task with their ipsilateral forepaw produced similar results as when animals used their contralateral forepaw (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from a control experiment examining motor contributions.

claim: Using a stimulus further into the temporal visual field (45–65° azimuth relative to midline) in PM produced similar or smaller magnitude effects as with the 25° eccentricity stimulus.
source: Using this stimulus, we found similar or smaller magnitude effects as with our 25° eccentricity stimulus (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), arguing that the weaker effects in PM relative to lateral areas were not due to the location of the visual stimulus.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with varied stimulus positions.

claim: Distance between the non-V1 spots and the V1 representation did not predict behavioral effect size.
source: Distance between the non-V1 spots and the V1 representation did not predict behavioral effect size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating the effects are due to inhibition at the site where the light was positioned.
evidence: This is an analysis of spatial specificity of behavioral effects.

claim: Moving the light spot between the V1 representation and LM/AL, within-subject, produced drastic falloff of behavioral effect relative to the V1 effect.
source: Second, we performed control experiments in which we moved the light spot between the V1 representation and LM/AL, within-subject, and found drastic falloff of behavioral effect relative to the V1 effect.
evidence: This is a finding from within-subject control experiments.

claim: The evoked visual response showed a spatial falloff consistent with, though slightly larger than, the light intensity patterns used.
source: We observed that the evoked visual response showed a spatial falloff consistent with, though slightly larger than, the light intensity patterns, or spots, that we used (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological characterization of spatial spread.

claim: The spatial extent of suppression in V1 was similar when V1 was directly activated and when LM/AL was inhibited, though the direct suppression was significantly stronger across V1 than feedback suppression.
source: These data confirmed that the spatial extent of suppression in V1 was similar when V1 was directly activated and when LM/AL was inhibited, though the direct suppression was significantly stronger across V1 than feedback suppression (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a comparison of spatial patterns from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Imaging V1 responses with L2/3-expressed GCaMP showed that the V1 representation was approximately the size of the area directly suppressed by the light spots.
source: Imaging V1 responses with L2/3-expressed GCaMP (Figure 6) also showed that the V1 representation was approximately the size of the area directly suppressed by our light spots, and that LM suppression affected an area of similar size.
evidence: This is a finding from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: LM suppression affected an area of similar size to the V1 representation.
source: Imaging V1 responses with L2/3-expressed GCaMP (Figure 6) also showed that the V1 representation was approximately the size of the area directly suppressed by our light spots, and that LM suppression affected an area of similar size.
evidence: This is a finding from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Inhibiting areas lateral to V1 (LM/AL and RL) produces the strongest effects on contrast-increment change detection, as large or larger than in V1.
source: In sum, inhibiting areas lateral to V1 (LM/AL and RL) produces the strongest effects on contrast-increment change detection, as large or larger than in V1.
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral findings comparing effect sizes across areas.

claim: The fact that some secondary visual areas (the lateral areas) show strong effects implies that V1 is not being directly decoded by remote areas.
source: The fact that some secondary visual areas (the lateral areas) show these strong effects implies that V1 is not being directly decoded by remote areas, but instead that information must pass through these secondary visual areas before being used for contrast-change detection.
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of behavioral effects across areas.

claim: Information must pass through secondary visual areas before being used for contrast-change detection.
source: The fact that some secondary visual areas (the lateral areas) show these strong effects implies that V1 is not being directly decoded by remote areas, but instead that information must pass through these secondary visual areas before being used for contrast-change detection.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral and physiological data.

claim: Lateral and medial areas have been shown to encode different features of visual stimuli, such as spatial or temporal frequencies.
source: Both lateral and medial areas have previously been shown to encode different features of visual stimuli, such as spatial or temporal frequencies (Andermann et al., 2011; Murakami et al., 2017), and thus might play a role in object identification or localization, as in the 'what' and 'where' pathways of the primate visual system (Mishkin and Ungerleider, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior physiological studies.

claim: PM does not seem to be involved in simple visual perceptual tasks.
source: In this case, lateral and medial areas might be representing different features of the visual world, and though PM does not seem to be involved in simple visual perceptual tasks, other types of behavioral decision-making might expose a role for PM (see Jin and Glickfeld, 2020).
evidence: This is an inference from the weak behavioral effects of PM inhibition.

claim: Siegle et al., 2019 constructed a hierarchy of visual areas based on electrophysiological data (LM→RL→LP→AL→PM→AM).
source: Siegle et al., 2019 constructed a hierarchy of visual areas based on electrophysiological data (LM→RL→LP→AL→PM→AM) and predicted that medial areas (PM/AM) were higher areas within the hierarchy, which serve to amplify or decode change-related signals.
evidence: This is a citation to a prior study proposing a hierarchical organization.

claim: The present data argue against the hypothesis that PM is downstream to V1 and lateral areas, at least in this task.
source: Our data argue against the hypothesis that PM is downstream to V1 and lateral areas, at least in this task.
evidence: This is an inference from the weak behavioral effects of PM inhibition.

claim: Jin and Glickfeld, 2020 found that lateral areas are involved in contrast-change detection tasks, and medial area (PM) inhibition has a smaller effect.
source: Jin and colleagues studied areas AL, LM, and PM and found, as we did, that lateral areas are involved in contrast-change detection tasks, and medial area (PM) inhibition has a smaller effect.
evidence: This is a citation to a recent study with similar findings.

claim: Jin and Glickfeld, 2020 found little or no change in sensitivity due to inhibiting PM, as the present study did.
source: While Jin and Glickfeld, 2020 found little or no change in sensitivity due to inhibiting PM, as we did, they found an effect on false alarm rates and criterion when PM was inhibited – and found shifts in false alarm rates for inhibiting PM both contra- and ipsilateral to the visual stimulus.
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from a prior study.

claim: Jin and Glickfeld, 2020 found an effect on false alarm rates and criterion when PM was inhibited.
source: While Jin and Glickfeld, 2020 found little or no change in sensitivity due to inhibiting PM, as we did, they found an effect on false alarm rates and criterion when PM was inhibited – and found shifts in false alarm rates for inhibiting PM both contra- and ipsilateral to the visual stimulus.
evidence: This is a citation to findings from a prior study that differ from the present results.

claim: Recent work has shown that mouse premotor cortex is involved in downstream processing of sensory signals.
source: Recent work has shown that mouse premotor cortex is involved in downstream processing of sensory signals (Wu et al., 2020; Zatka-Haas et al., 2020), but it has been unclear whether secondary visual areas are involved in all or most sensory tasks that involve V1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Evidence for choice or decision signals has been found in areas including frontal and premotor cortex and the striatum, but not in either V1 or secondary areas.
source: Evidence for choice or decision signals has been found in areas including frontal and premotor cortex and the striatum, but not in either V1 or secondary areas (Steinmetz et al., 2019), arguing that the decoding happens outside both V1 and the secondary areas.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Deficits in visual detection similar to those observed in this study are also seen when the mouse SC is inhibited.
source: A more likely alternative hypothesis to the sequential interpretation is that multiple brain areas are read out together in parallel. Deficits in visual detection similar to those we observed are also seen when the mouse SC is inhibited (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study of SC function.

claim: The primary thalamic V1 feedforward source, the LGN, projects strongly to area PM and sparsely to area LM.
source: The primary thalamic V1 feedforward source, the LGN, projects strongly to area PM and sparsely to area LM (Bienkowski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the NIH Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) and complied with Public Health Service policy on the humane care and use of laboratory animals.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the NIH Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) and complied with Public Health Service policy on the humane care and use of laboratory animals.
evidence: This is a statement of ethical compliance.

claim: VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice (N = 16) were used for behavioral and electrophysiology experiments.
source: VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice (ChR2 targeted at the Slc32a1 locus, Zhao et al., 2011, Jax stock no. 014548, N = 16) were used for behavioral and electrophysiology experiments.
evidence: This describes the mouse line and sample size used.

claim: Tamoxifen-treated Ai148;Cux2-CreERT2 mice (N = 3) were used for imaging experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
source: Tamoxifen-treated Ai148;Cux2-CreERT2 mice (N = 3, GCaMP6f targeted at the Igs7 locus and CreERT2 targeted at the Cux2 locus, respectively, Daigle et al., 2018; Jax stock No. 030328, MRRC stock no. 032779-MU) were used for imaging experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This describes the mouse line and sample size used for specific experiments.

claim: A PV-Cre;ReaChR-mCitrine mouse was used for LM inhibition during widefield GCaMP imaging in Figure 6.
source: A PV-Cre;ReaChR-mCitrine mouse (Cre targeted at the Pvalb locus and ReaChR targeted at the Gt(ROSA)26Sor locus; Lin et al., 2013; Jax stock nos. 008069 and 024846, respectively) was used for LM inhibition during widefield GCaMP imaging in Figure 6.
evidence: This describes the mouse line used for specific experiments.

claim: Nine females and eleven males were used in total, singly housed on a reverse light/dark cycle.
source: Nine females and eleven males were used in total, singly housed on a reverse light/dark cycle.
evidence: This describes the sex distribution and housing conditions of experimental animals.

claim: A 5 mm diameter craniotomy was made, centered over V1 (−3.1 mm ML, +1.5 mm AP from lambda).
source: Using aseptic technique, a titanium headpost was affixed using C and B Metabond (Parkell) and a 5 mm diameter craniotomy was made, centered over V1 (−3.1 mm ML, +1.5 mm AP from lambda).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure and coordinates used.

claim: For experiments involving widefield calcium imaging during LM inhibition, AAV9-hSyn-jGCaMP7s was diluted 1:9 in sterile PBS and injected 300 µm below the surface of the brain.
source: For experiments involving widefield calcium imaging during LM inhibition, AAV9-hSyn-jGCaMP7s was diluted 1:9 in sterile PBS and injected 300 µm below the surface of the brain.
evidence: This describes the viral injection procedure for imaging experiments.

claim: Multiple 800 nL injections were done at 200 nL/min to achieve widespread coverage across the 5 mm window.
source: Multiple 800 nL injections were done at 200 nL/min to achieve widespread coverage across the 5 mm window.
evidence: This describes the injection parameters used.

claim: Hemodynamic-related changes in absorption were measured by measuring reflected 530 nm light.
source: To determine the location of V1 and surrounding visual areas, we delivered small visual stimuli to head-fixed animals at different retinotopic positions and measured hemodynamic-related changes in absorption by measuring reflected 530 nm light (Schuett et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the imaging method used for area localization.

claim: Upward-drifting square wave gratings (2 Hz, 0.1 cycles/degree) masked with a raised cosine window (10° diameter) were presented at different retinotopic locations for 5 s with 10 s of mean luminance between each trial.
source: We presented upward-drifting square wave gratings (2 Hz, 0.1 cycles/degree) masked with a raised cosine window (10° diameter) at different retinotopic locations for 5 s with 10 s of mean luminance between each trial.
evidence: This describes the visual stimuli used for retinotopic mapping.

claim: The hemodynamic response to each stimulus was calculated as the change in reflectance of the cortical surface between the baseline period and a response window starting 2–3 s after stimulus onset.
source: The hemodynamic response to each stimulus was calculated as the change in reflectance of the cortical surface between the baseline period and a response window starting 2–3 s after stimulus onset, corresponding to the previously reported time course of visually evoked hemodynamic responses in mouse V1 (Heimel et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the analysis method for hemodynamic imaging data.

claim: An average visual area map was created based on data from Zhuang et al., 2017 and Garrett et al., 2014, and fit to the cortex based on the centroids of each stimulus' V1 hemodynamic response.
source: We created an average visual area map, based on data from Zhuang et al., 2017 and Garrett et al., 2014, and fit it to the cortex based on the centroids of each stimulus' V1 hemodynamic response.
evidence: This describes the method for fitting area maps to individual animals.

claim: Green fluorescence images were captured using an eGFP filter, at an average frame rate of 10 Hz for 150 stimulus presentations.
source: Green fluorescence images were captured using an eGFP filter, at an average frame rate of 10 Hz (one stimulus frame followed by 32 post-stimulus frames, 4 × 4 binning) for 150 stimulus presentations.
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters for GCaMP experiments.

claim: A 10 µL water reward was given randomly (10% probability) to keep animals awake and alert during GCaMP imaging.
source: A 10 µL water reward was given randomly (10% probability) to keep animals awake and alert.
evidence: This describes a procedural detail to maintain animal alertness.

claim: The first principal component, which encoded global fluctuation of the entire frame, was discarded in GCaMP imaging analysis.
source: For GCaMP imaging with PV-ReaChR inactivation in LM/AL (Figure 6; AAV-GCaMP7s), we decomposed the imaging data using principal components analysis (PCA), discarded the first component, which encoded global fluctuation of the entire frame, and reconstructed the image stack.
evidence: This describes the analysis method for GCaMP imaging data.

claim: Mice were required to press a lever for a maximum of 4.1 s in the behavioral task.
source: Mice were required to press a lever for a maximum of 4.1 s.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the behavioral task.

claim: At a random time point during the trial, after a fixed period of 400 ms where the stimulus could not appear, a small Gabor patch (+25° azimuth, 0° elevation, 14° FWHM, spatial frequency 0.1 cycle/degree) was presented for 100 ms.
source: At a random time point during this period, after a fixed period of 400 ms where the stimulus could not appear, a small Gabor patch (+25° azimuth, 0° elevation, 14° FWHM, spatial frequency 0.1 cycle/degree) was presented for 100 ms.
evidence: This describes the visual stimulus parameters in the behavioral task.

claim: Animals had 550 ms to report the stimulus by releasing the lever.
source: Animals had 550 ms to report the stimulus by releasing the lever.
evidence: This describes the response window in the behavioral task.

claim: Trials resulting in hits were rewarded with 1.5–3 µL liquid reward.
source: Trials resulting in hits were rewarded with 1.5–3 µL liquid reward.
evidence: This describes the reward parameters in the behavioral task.

claim: Mean session length was 384 ± 97 trials.
source: Sessions lasted until the animal reached its daily water supplement or until the animal stopped on its own, whichever came first (mean session length = 384 ± 97 trials).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of behavioral session length.

claim: Fiber optic cannulae (400 µm core diameter, 425 µm outer diameter, 0.39 NA) were cemented above specific cortical areas.
source: Fiber optic cannulae (400 µm core diameter, 425 µm outer diameter, 0.39 NA, Thorlabs CFMLC14L02) were cemented above specific cortical areas as determined by hemodynamic intrinsic imaging retinotopic maps.
evidence: This describes the optogenetic hardware used.

claim: Light spot size and intensity contours were found by measuring the FWHM of the illuminated area (spot area mean ± SEM, 0.42 ± 0.13 mm2, N = 34 spots).
source: Light spot size and intensity contours were found by measuring the FWHM of the illuminated area (spot area mean ± SEM, 0.42 ± 0.13 mm2, N = 34 spots; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative characterization of optogenetic light spots.

claim: The LED pulse train was on for 200 ms and off for 1000 ms.
source: Once animals were performing well on the visual task and we had a full psychometric curve, we introduced a pulsed LED (on for 200 ms, off for 1000 ms) to each trial.
evidence: This describes the optogenetic stimulation parameters.

claim: On 50% of trials, the visual stimulus was presented 55 ms before the last LED pulse in the train (ON trials).
source: On 50% of trials, the visual stimulus was presented 55 ms before the last LED pulse in the train (ON trials).
evidence: This describes the timing of ON trials in the behavioral task.

claim: On the remaining 50% of trials, the visual stimulus was presented 180 ms before the last LED pulse (OFF trials).
source: On the remaining 50% of trials, the visual stimulus was presented 180 ms before the last LED pulse (OFF trials).
evidence: This describes the timing of OFF trials in the behavioral task.

claim: OFF trials were slightly longer than ON trials (ON: 1454 ms ± 187, mean ± SD trial length, OFF: 1942 ms ± 261 ms).
source: Because of this, OFF trials were slightly longer than ON trials (ON: 1454 ms ± 187, mean ± SD trial length, OFF: 1942 ms ± 261 ms), though hazard rates for the two kinds of trials were nearly identical (Figure 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of trial lengths between conditions.

claim: Only sessions with lapse rates <20% and sufficient trials at each contrast (average 10 trials per contrast level, per ON/OFF trial type) were included for analysis.
source: To exclude experimental sessions with insufficient data or where animals had poor motivation, only sessions with lapse rates <20% and sufficient trials at each contrast (average 10 trials per contrast level, per ON/OFF trial type) were included for further analysis (579 sessions total; 170 excluded, 409 sessions included).
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for behavioral data analysis.

claim: 579 sessions total were collected, with 170 excluded and 409 sessions included in the analysis.
source: To exclude experimental sessions with insufficient data or where animals had poor motivation, only sessions with lapse rates <20% and sufficient trials at each contrast (average 10 trials per contrast level, per ON/OFF trial type) were included for further analysis (579 sessions total; 170 excluded, 409 sessions included).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the data set.

claim: A multisite silicon probe electrode (NeuroNexus; 32-site model 4 × 8-100-200-177; four shank, eight sites/shank) was used for electrophysiological recordings.
source: We targeted a multisite silicon probe electrode (NeuroNexus; 32-site model 4 × 8-100-200-177; four shank, eight sites/shank; sites electrochemically coated with PEDOT:PSS [poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene): poly(styrenesulfonate)]) to the center of the LED spot using a micromanipulator (MPC-200, Sutter Instruments).
evidence: This describes the recording hardware used.

claim: After insertion of the probes so that the deepest site was 500 µm below the dural surface, experimenters waited 30–60 min without moving the probes to reduce slow drift and provide more stable recordings.
source: After insertion of the probes so that the deepest site was 500 µm below the dural surface, we waited 30–60 min without moving the probes to reduce slow drift and provide more stable recordings.
evidence: This describes the recording procedure.

claim: The visual stimulus (90% contrast Gabor, 100 ms duration) was presented on every trial, paired with a 200 ms LED pulse at varying intensity (180 reps each intensity).
source: The visual stimulus (90% contrast Gabor, 100 ms duration, same as during behavioral experiments) was presented on every trial, paired with a 200 ms LED pulse at varying intensity (180 reps each intensity).
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters for electrophysiology experiments.

claim: A 1 µL water reward was randomly provided on 5% of the stimulus trials to keep animals awake and alert during recordings.
source: To keep animals awake and alert, animals were water-scheduled and a 1 µL water reward was randomly provided on 5% of the stimulus trials.
evidence: This describes a procedural detail to maintain animal alertness.

claim: Single units had SNR of 3.5 ± 0.36 (mean ± SD, N = 171 units) and multiunit SNR was 3.1 ± 0.28 (mean ± SD, N = 54 units).
source: Single units had SNR (Kelly et al., 2007; Histed, 2018; Sanzeni et al., 2020) of 3.5 ± 0.36 (mean ± SD, N = 171 units) and multiunit SNR was 3.1 ± 0.28 (mean ± SD, N = 54 units).
evidence: This is a quantitative characterization of recording quality.

claim: Multi units were excluded from further analysis.
source: Multi units were excluded from further analysis.
evidence: This describes an analysis decision.
